segments.text: Taking a picture on your phone is usually effortless.
You open the app, point, and tap the button.
For most situations, the default settings work perfectly.
But sometimes the environment requires an adjustment.
If you're trying to capture a family portrait at dusk,
the standard settings leave everyone in shadows.
You have to turn on the flash.
Or if you're sitting high up in the stands at a hockey game,
trying to capture your favorite player on the ice,
the default view is too wide, so you zoom in.
You don't change these camera settings for every single picture,
but knowing when to activate them helps you get exactly what you want.
Artificial intelligence apps operate the same way.
The default mode handles most tasks, but depending on the app,
you often have three distinct choices to adjust.
The model, the thinking, and the research.
You won't need to tweak these settings every time you write a prompt,
but understanding what they actually do
allows you to approach your work with intention,
returning much better answers.
When you use an AI app,
a large language model, or LLM, powers its responses.
You can think of the LLM as the engine inside a vehicle.
It dictates the base capacity of the application.
When a specific app gives you a choice of which model to use,
you are essentially opening the hood and swapping out that engine
for one built with different capabilities.
This board outlines two main choices.
The everyday model handles quick questions,
like suggesting a funny movie.
The more capable model tackles demanding tasks,
like planning a business with costs and pricing.
The bottom banner highlights best practice.
Start with the default and upgrade only when needed.
Upgrading your model increases the raw intellectual horsepower
applied to your prompt.
That is the necessary first step when handling complex work.
Choosing a model changes the engine you use.
The next variable, thinking, adjusts something different.
How much time the AI spends working through your task
before it starts typing?
Consider how you approach an English exam.
Before writing the essay, you decide what to say,
gather examples, and organize an outline.
The AI isn't experiencing thoughts the way a human does,
but the thinking mode serves a similar mechanical purpose.
It forces the system to pause and process intermediate steps
instead of immediately generating a response.
This interface shows two modes.
Less thinking spends minimal time,
excelling at routine work like formatting meeting notes.
More thinking forces the AI to weigh options
and verify logic for analytical tasks,
like scheduling a project team.
The bottom directive is clear.
Give AI more time for sequential steps.
Giving the system extra time to evaluate sequential logic
reduces errors when you need to balance competing constraints
like scheduling conflicts or resource limits.
The final variable you can control is the depth of research.
Stopping at a drive-through for a cheeseburger
means you already know enough to order.
It's a quick transaction requiring zero external data.
Buying your first house requires a completely different approach.
You actively gather information,
compare neighborhood pricing,
and calculate driving distances before making a decision.
This graphic breaks down two levels of investigation.
Regular chat answers single questions quickly,
like comparing driving times between cities.
Deep research triggers a wider sweep,
gathering data across websites to build a sourced report,
needed for comparing specific university programs.
Activate this to compare conflicting information across sources.
Activating this mode instructs the AI to pull raw data from external websites
and synthesize those distinct facts into a single unified document.
Model, thinking, research.
Use them when the work demands more.
You do not need to maximize every setting for every prompt.
Matching the level of capability, processing time,
and investigation to this specific problem
ensures the output matches your exact requirements.
